problems.title: Equation (4) is a table probability, not the claimed Fisher p-value
claim: Section 3.2, p. 5, states, in paraphrase, that Fisher’s test returns the probability of the observed contingency table or a more extreme table under independence. Equation (4) then defines
analysis: For a \(2\times2\) table with every cell equal to \(2\), the feasible conditional masses are \((1,16,36,16,1)/70\). The observed mass is \(18/35\), but every feasible table is no more probable, so the probability-ordered two-sided Fisher p-value is \(1\). Equation (4) prints one hypergeometric mass, not the stated tail. The released algorithm does include tail summation, which limits the impact of this printed-formula discrepancy.
result: The displayed statistic is not its stated p-value, but the released algorithm already performs the missing tail summation in principle, limiting the finding to the printed specification.
repair: Replace the single mass with the specified probability-ordered tail: sum \(\binom{s}{k}\binom{n-s}{r-k}/\binom nr\) over feasible \(k\) whose numerator weight is no larger than the observed one. The existing code’s tail operation is affirmative counterevidence against assuming it trained on the literal single mass.
problems.impact_rationale: The displayed statistic is not its stated p-value, but the released algorithm already performs the missing tail summation in principle, limiting the finding to the printed specification.
problems.existing_correction_status: The local formula, numerical or scope proposal is retained; current cited passages and author-source paths still contain the relevant behavior. Author adoption is unestablished.

problems.title: Float32 ties and the exact-\(p=1\) gate change the released association score
problems.source_location: Eq. (5), PDF p. 5; released Fisher-tail routine and exact-p-equals-one gate.
claim: Released compute_key_tokens.py, fisher_exact_test, lines 26–51, computes masses using float32 log-gamma expressions and selects terms by literal probability comparison. Lines 157–159 apply the exact \(p\ne1\) gate corresponding to Eq. (5).
analysis: For table \(\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\2&9\end{pmatrix}\), the exact feasible masses are \(11/24,11/24,1/12\), so the two-sided p-value is \(1\). Rounding can separate the equal masses and exclude one tied term. Separately, a rounded value \(1.000000119\) fails the exact equality gate and maps to approximately \(e^{-2p}=0.1353\) instead of zero. These are distinct source-level numerical failure mechanisms; previously reported native outputs are historical.
result: Float32 tie comparisons and the discontinuous endpoint gate can distort token scores; actual training frequencies, CUDA rounding and downstream effects remain unmeasured.
repair: Compare exact integer hypergeometric numerator weights to preserve equal-probability ties, then apply an explicitly specified endpoint rule. This local statistic correction does not establish an improvement in training accuracy.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: Float32 tie comparisons and the discontinuous endpoint gate can distort token scores; actual training frequencies, CUDA rounding and downstream effects remain unmeasured.

problems.title: The released token bonus has different weights and scale from Eq. (10)
claim: Equation (10), p. 6, specifies the additive bonus
analysis: The released default maps \((F,IG,D)\) to \(2[\operatorname{sigmoid}((F+IG)D/2)-1/2]\), whereas Eq. (10) with the appendix weights uses \(\operatorname{sigmoid}((F+2IG)D)-1/2\). Their ranges are \((-1,1)\) and \((-1/2,1/2)\), respectively, so they cannot be algebraically equivalent. Both give zero at \(D=0\); that matching control does not establish equivalence elsewhere.
result: The current bonus has different relative coefficients and output range; this defeats exact reconstruction of the printed contract without proving reported accuracies false.
repair: Identify the actually trained canonical variant, then either document the released coefficients, normalization and range or align the implementation with Eq. (10). No empirical choice between these variants is established.
problems.impact_rationale: The current bonus has different relative coefficients and output range; this defeats exact reconstruction of the printed contract without proving reported accuracies false.

problems.title: The directional score is undefined for permitted zero-frequency cases unless a boundary rule is added
claim: Section 3.4, Eq. (9), PDF p. 6, defines \(D=\arcsin\sqrt{a/(a+c)}-\arcsin\sqrt{b/(b+d)}+h_3(TF_T/TF_F-TF_F/TF_T)\). Algorithm 1 applies it to tokens in the union of sampled rollouts without requiring positive frequency in each outcome group.
analysis: Use four correct rollouts containing the token and four incorrect rollouts not containing it. Both outcome groups exist, but \(TF_T>0\) and \(TF_F=0\). The arcsine term is \(\pi/2\), while \(TF_T/TF_F\) is undefined over the reals. A finite regularization or extended-real limiting convention is an additional definition; it does not follow from the printed formula.

The current source adds \(10^{-5}\) in frequency denominators and \(10^{-10}\) in class-proportion denominators, and returns zero when either outcome group is empty. These protections resolve a runtime boundary in the release; the supported concern is the printed contract’s omission of that regularization.
result: The formula is incomplete at allowed zero frequencies, while current code already supplies numerical safeguards; this is a local documentation/domain discrepancy.
repair: State the denominator regularization and empty-group branches used by the implementation. Alternative smoothing requires an explicit changed definition; no empirical effect is claimed.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The no-length-penalty and joint efficiency statements require narrower scope
problems.source_location: Introduction, PDF p. 2; Section 2.3, PDF p. 4; Table 2, PDF p. 8; Appendix G.3, PDF p. 19.
claim: The introduction, p. 2, and discussion of Table 2, p. 8, describe reduced response length without a length-penalty reward. Section 2.3, p. 4, explicitly describes DAPO overlong reward shaping. Appendix G.3, p. 19, sets an overlong buffer of \(512\) and a length-penalty coefficient of 1.0.
analysis: The current \(7\)-billion-parameter DAPO launch enables a \(512\)-token overlong buffer, maximum length \(3072\), and penalty coefficient \(1\). The reward code adds \(\min(-(L-2560)/512,0)\), so lengths \(2816\) and \(3072\) receive penalties \(-1/2\) and \(-1\). KTAE can add no new penalty while inheriting DAPO’s existing penalty; that narrower interpretation remains coherent.

The current tables give \(7\)-billion-parameter GRPO+KTAE mean accuracy \(51.7\) and length \(718.6\), versus DAPO+KTAE accuracy \(52.5\) and length \(777.2\), so the two extrema belong to different variants. Both beat their base algorithms in mean length; the \(1.5\)-billion-parameter DAPO+KTAE variant has both displayed extrema. Individual MATH500 lengths nevertheless increase from \(635\) to \(884\) and \(617\) to \(983\). These are qualifications of combined-system, average and variant scope, not corrected benchmark measurements.
result: Supported configuration and inference-scope qualification; no new efficiency measurements were obtained.
repair: State that KTAE adds no separate length penalty, disclose inherited DAPO reward shaping, and identify which model variant attains each accuracy/length extremum. Distinguish mean response length from every-benchmark length and from latency.
problems.impact_rationale: The reward configuration and different extrema require narrower efficiency wording; favorable average-length comparisons remain, and no new latency or accuracy result is inferred.
